planting.note: Seed benefits from a period of cold, moist stratification, so fall sowing outdoors or several weeks of refrigerated stratification ahead of a spring sowing improves germination; established plants also self-sow readily in open ground.

directions: Pale beardtongue is a slender, clump-forming native perennial of dry meadows, open woodland edges, and limestone glades across the central and eastern United States, from the Great Lakes south into the mid-South and west onto the eastern Great Plains. Narrow basal leaves give rise to wiry flowering stems topped with loose spikes of small, pale lavender-white to nearly white tubular flowers lined with faint purple nectar guides, opening in late spring and attracting bees and other small pollinators. It thrives in lean, well-drained soil, including rocky or gravelly sites, and is less tolerant of rich, consistently moist garden beds than some of its showier relatives. Use it in native meadow plantings, dry prairie restorations, or informal cottage borders where its airy, understated flowers can mix with other short-grass prairie species.
sources: Lady Bird Johnson Wildflower Center — Native Plant Database

planting.note: Seed germinates best after a cold, moist stratification period, so sow outdoors in fall or stratify in a refrigerator for 60-90 days before a spring sowing.

directions: Sidebells penstemon is a shortgrass-prairie and foothills native of the central and southern Rockies, found on dry, gravelly slopes and open grassland from Wyoming and Colorado south into New Mexico. Its common name comes from the distinctive one-sided (secund) arrangement of its sky-blue to lavender-pink tubular flowers, which all face the same direction along the upper stem, opening in mid to late spring well before most summer-blooming beardtongues. Waxy, blue-gray basal foliage and a tidy clumping habit make it a good fit for xeriscape beds, gravel gardens, and native shortgrass meadow plantings. It demands sharp drainage and resents heavy, wet, or richly amended soil, performing best in lean, rocky, or sandy ground in full sun.

planting.note: Seed benefits from 60-90 days of cold, moist stratification; sow outdoors in fall or stratify in a refrigerator before a spring sowing for best germination.

directions: Fuzzytongue penstemon is a low, mounding native of dry plains, badlands, and rocky foothills across the Great Plains and Intermountain West, from the Dakotas and Montana south into Colorado and Utah. Its large, pale lavender to pink-purple flowers are among the showiest of the shorter beardtongues, and each bloom reveals a conspicuously dense, golden-orange, hairy staminode protruding from the throat, the 'fuzzy tongue' that gives the species its name and that bumblebees use as a landing platform. Plants form tight, woody-based clumps of gray-green foliage well suited to rock gardens, gravel beds, and dry native plantings where soil stays lean and fast-draining. It is intolerant of summer humidity, heavy clay, or overhead irrigation, and performs best in neglect once established.

common_name: Pikes Peak Purple Penstemon (Compact Purple Hybrid Beardtongue)

planting.note: Propagated by division or cuttings rather than seed, since it is a hybrid cultivar; set out container plants in spring once soil has warmed, in gritty, fast-draining soil.

directions: A Plant Select introduction bred for Front Range xeriscape gardens, this compact Mexicali hybrid forms a tidy mound of narrow, slightly glossy foliage covered through late spring and summer in a profusion of rich violet-purple tubular flowers that draw hummingbirds and bumblebees alike. It shares the same tough, drought-tolerant hybrid vigor as its sibling selection 'Red Rocks' but offers a deeper purple flower color, and like other Mexicali-group penstemons it tolerates both the dry summers and sharply drained winter soils of the Intermountain West better than most eastern species. Deadheading spent spikes encourages a strong rebloom cycle into fall. Grow in lean, gritty, well-drained soil in full sun; it resents heavy clay, poor drainage, and wet winter feet.
sources: Plant Select (Colorado State University / Denver Botanic Gardens)
